DATA CENTER OPERATIONS: COMMISSIONING THE FACILITY IS ONLY THE BEGINNING.

A hyperscale AI data center can pass L1–L5 commissioning and Integrated Systems Testing (IST).

But what happens the day after turnover?

That is where the Director of Data Center Operations becomes accountable.

Construction delivers the infrastructure. Commissioning verifies its performance. Operations must sustain that performance 24/7 while equipment ages, workloads change, maintenance occurs, and failures happen.

A director is not there to personally operate every breaker, repair every chiller, or write every MOP.

The job is to build and lead the organization that keeps the facility safe, available, and financially controlled.

WHAT DOES THAT REQUIRE?

1. RELIABILITY: Monitor critical loads, redundancy, alarms, and degraded operating conditions. A facility can be online and still be one failure away from an outage.

2. PEOPLE: Maintain qualified 24/7 staffing, clear escalation authority, training, and shift accountability.

3. MAINTENANCE: Control preventive maintenance, asset condition, spare parts, OEM support, and deferred-work risks.

4. PROCEDURES: Govern SOPs, MOPs, EOPs, switching activities, and changes to live systems.

5. INCIDENT RESPONSE: Establish command, stabilize operations, communicate impacts, recover safely, and address root causes.

6. CAPACITY AND COOLING: Track electrical headroom, IT load, chilled-water performance, CDU availability, flow, temperature, and thermal redundancy.

7. BUSINESS PERFORMANCE: Manage OpEx, CapEx, vendor contracts, customer commitments, and measurable operating KPIs.

HERE IS THE EXECUTION GAP.

Too many organizations treat substantial completion or successful IST as proof that the facility is operationally ready.

It is not enough.

Before accepting turnover, operations needs approved procedures, trained personnel, verified alarms, accurate as-builts, maintenance plans, critical spares, closed high-risk deficiencies, and documented ownership of remaining risks.

A generator that passed its load-bank test can still fail months later.

A CDU that passed functional testing can still develop a flow or water-quality problem.

A UPS can support the load while its redundancy is compromised.

THE DIRECTOR MUST IDENTIFY THE RISK BEFORE THE CUSTOMER EXPERIENCES THE OUTAGE.

THE REAL DIFFERENCE:

Commissioning asks: Does the system perform as designed?

Operations asks: Can we keep it performing safely, reliably, and efficiently every single day?

DATA CENTER OWNERS: ARE YOU HIRING OPERATIONS DIRECTORS TO MANAGE FACILITIES OR SIMPLY TO REACT WHEN SOMETHING BREAKS?

A recruiting tool launched this week promising to go from job description to booked interview in under five minutes, running "autonomously, 24x7," no contract needed. Its pitch line stuck with me: hiring at the speed AI now writes code, in minutes instead of months.

We have run our own hiring agent at Sunday for thirteen weeks, held to the same 90-day bar as a new human hire. The fastest thing we built in that stretch is also the one I regret most.

Early on we let it shortlist candidates off one automated call, no human listening in, to cut shortlist time in half. It worked, for a while. Then a hiring manager caught it waving through someone who had clearly rehearsed answers off a script, the kind of thing a recruiter catches from tone alone in ninety seconds. We put a human back in that loop. Shortlist time went right back up.

So when a company advertises an agent running that fast with nobody checking in, I believe the speed. I don't yet believe the accuracy comes free with it.

Maybe I'm wrong, and five minutes is enough once the model is good enough. Where would you draw the line between automating a hiring step and still needing a human inside it?

An AI chip can stay in a Malaysian data centre while a customer overseas uses its computing power. How do you trace who has access?
That question stood out to me as a semiconductor recruiter in Malaysia. On 18 November, Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said Malaysia was seeking clarification from the US on licensing requirements for advanced AI chips and how the restrictions apply when data centres provide computing capacity to third parties. Malaysia is also investigating alleged chip re-exports. Johari said he had yet to see documents showing that data centre tenants had traded or re-exported the chips. 
From a hiring perspective, those are two different tracing problems. A supply chain specialist can follow a GPU from its shipping declaration to the rack where it was installed. To understand who can use that GPU, a cloud engineer may need to connect access permissions and usage records to the customer account. Each team holds a different part of the answer.
That changes what I’d ask in an interview. For someone working in AI infrastructure, one question I’d put on the table is “If a customer’s contract ended today, how would you verify that their access to the GPU cluster had ended too?”
The answer would tell me how the engineer thinks about access controls, what evidence they trust, and how they work with the people managing the customer relationship. Those are skills I’d look for as Malaysia’s data centre sector works through the implications of these rules.
For those working in Malaysia’s semiconductor supply chain or data centres, where is the bigger challenge in your experience — tracking the hardware or verifying who can use it?

Small and midsize businesses just posted their lowest confidence reading on record. They also kept hiring. Both things are true, and the second one is the story.

Principal's October index shows what employers actually did in 2026. Of the 89% that made operational adjustments, 93% developed or redeployed people they already had through cross-training, upskilling and internal moves. 72% brought in flexible or specialized talent. 58% changed how the work itself gets done with AI and automation.

98% of the employers who changed how work gets done report at least one meaningful result. 51% cite better productivity and efficiency, 41% report more consistent, higher-quality work. The employers that made several of these changes together report the best outcomes.

That is the playbook the cautious half is running. Here is where each move breaks when it is done badly.

Upskilling without a target is a training budget with no return. If you cannot name the two roles the program is meant to fill in 12 months, you are funding general education and calling it a pipeline.

Flexible talent without scoping becomes a rotating door. Contract and project hires fail on unclear outcomes far more often than on skill. Write down what belongs to them and what stays with the team before the req goes out.

Automation aimed at headcount rather than at the task backfires. The 41% reporting higher-quality work are the ones who automated a specific, repetitive step. Teams that automate a role instead of a task usually spend the savings on rework.

And keep the benefits. Only 3% of employers cut or eliminated a benefit this year, and 8% plan to add one in 2027. That is the cheapest retention decision available right now.

The most confident-looking hiring plan in your market may be less deliberate than yours. The question is whether yours is deliberate enough to show up in the numbers.

I've said all that to say this: Over the last week and a half or so I have been going through interviews with a great  company, one whose mission is personally very important to me. I don't want to name the place yet, as this is still on-going, but hopefully those folks see this at some point in the future and realize how positively impactful the way they conduct their hiring process is. To them: thank you.

Thoughts on Higher Ed B2B in 2027

Partnership is a meaningless word in a business context. It means “we are under contract and don’t trust you” as much as it means “we do.”

Strip away the label and look at the actual markers of a partnership. On the surface, it’s KPIs and ROI. Beneath that are defined objectives and a shared belief in the solution. And at the very bottom, holding all of it up, is trust.

Why bother going here? Because selling into higher ed has always required slowing down before a deal gets signed. It’s that "feeling you out" stage where two organizations get on the same page. And that dynamic is about to get a lot more intense.

We saw it in hiring first. It’s almost useless to send a resume anymore. Candidates use AI to customize 10,000 resumes to 10,000 job descriptions, and institutions use AI to write the descriptions and vet the applicants. The cycle is a snake eating its own tail.

One provost told me recently that hiring an outside vendor now requires a slowing down on par with hiring an employee, which means far more extensive, in-person vetting than in the past. 

In higher ed, faculty are wrestling with how AI has disrupted authentic assessment, forcing a return to oral defenses and live demonstration because written work is too easily faked. 

Vendor evaluation is on that exact same path. Great case studies, polished demos, and RFP responses are now flooded with AI-generated perfection, making it harder than ever to spot real trust signals.

What AI is doing to authentic assessment in the classroom, it’s also doing to old-fashioned discernment in the buying process.

That said, higher ed has a path toward decision-making that is centuries old: deliberation and discernment. It turns out the bureaucracy can move remarkably fast when given a clear objective. 

I’ve seen curriculum written in weeks, AI policies signed off on by 18 committees inside four months, and new AI centers built for administrators and students in even shorter periods.

At the core of institutional change is trust and transparency. In my work with clients, deals get stuck, and companies stay trapped in pilot purgatory, for the exact same reason. They skipped the trust step.

If you’ve ever wondered how a founder at a company no bigger than yours moves effortlessly through a room full of provosts, how a sales leader lands on a panel with presidents, or how a marketing leader assembles a webinar with your exact ICP while you can’t even get in the door, this is why.

They put in the reps. They showed up to listen before they pitched, and they did the slowing down to speed up.

CNCP, Chinese companies are winning $200 million contracts in Saudi Arabia’s energy sector. The headline numbers look impressive. But the contract structure is what actually determines how much money you make.
 
I see this pattern repeatedly when Chinese companies enter the Saudi oilfield services market: they win on price and technical capability, then discover the economics don’t work the way they expected. Usually because of three things they underestimated at the bid stage.
 
Equipment sale vs. operated service contract.
 
These are fundamentally different business models. An equipment sale is a one-time revenue recognition event. An operated service contract — where you supply the rig and the crew and get paid by the day or by performance — is recurring revenue that compounds over the contract term. The same headline contract value means very different things to your P&L and cash flow depending on which structure you’re in. Many Chinese companies default to the equipment sale model because it’s familiar. The Saudi market increasingly rewards the service model, but it comes with real operational obligations on the ground.
 
ICV requirements are contract terms, not background noise.
 
Saudi Aramco’s In-Country Value (iktva) program is built into contracts. Your score affects whether you win future work. It measures local content in goods and services, salaries paid to Saudi nationals, training spend, and supplier development. If you bid a Saudi oilfield contract without modeling your ICV obligations — local hiring ratios, local procurement commitments, training budgets — you are bidding on incomplete information. The localization cost is real and needs to be in your numbers from day one.
 
Equipment import: customs and VAT have specific rules.
 
Saudi Arabia has provisions for temporary import of equipment used in oil and gas projects, but the process requires proper documentation and the right HS code classification from the start. VAT treatment on imported equipment used in qualifying energy projects has its own rules. Getting this wrong at entry creates problems that are expensive to unwind.
 
Same contract value. Very different outcomes depending on how you structured it.

Hiring - FDE Applied AI Developer
Location: Chantilly, VA(Remote)
Job type - contract 

JOB DESCRIPTION:
Job responsibilities
Serve as the lead developer for complex Google Gemini, transitioning from rapid prototypes to production-grade agentic workflows (e.g., multi-agent systems, MCP servers) that drive measurable ROI.
Architect and code conversational flows that are not just functional but optimized for the "connective tissue" between Google’s Gemini AI products and customers’ live infrastructure, including APIs, legacy data silos, and security perimeters.
Build high-performance evaluation (Eval) pipelines and observability frameworks to optimize complex agentic workloads, focusing on reasoning loops, tool selection, and reducing latency while maintaining production-grade security and networking.
Identify repeatable field patterns and technical "friction points" in Google’s AAI stack, converting them into reusable modules or product feature requests for Engineering teams.
Co-build with customer engineering teams to instill Google-grade development best practices, ensuring long-term project success and high end-user adoption.

Key skills:- 

10 years of experience with software development using Python or similar coding languages.
Experience architecting AI systems on cloud platforms (e.g., GCP).
Experience deploying resources via Terraform or similar tools to automate the setup of agents, functions, or networking.
Experience building full-stack applications that interact with enterprise IT infrastructures and developing external customer projects.

Please share relevant resume with linked-in id at - monti.kumar@neerinfo.com

🔹 Location: Remote
🔹 Duration: Contract

We're looking for a hands-on AI Engineer to build and deploy production-grade AI applications that solve real business problems.

What You'll Do
✅ Build multi-agent and tool-using AI applications over enterprise data

✔ RAG, retrieval quality evaluation, and AI testing frameworks
✔ SQL, Pandas, and strong data validation skills
✔ Cloud deployment experience (AWS, Azure, or GCP)
✔ Understanding of AI security, prompt injection prevention, and safe tool execution

⭐ Nice to Have Healthcare Data (FHIR/HL7, HIPAA), Knowledge Graphs, Neo4j, Bedrock AgentCore, Vertex AI, Azure Foundry, Terraform, LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, vLLM.

If you've built AI products that are actively used by real users and can demonstrate measurable impact, we'd love to connect.
